newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai military to comply with spending cut order.
newsitem.headline: Thai military to comply with spending cut order.

text.p: Thailand's influential military will comply with a government policy to cut spending but officials said on Wednesday the armed forces will still make spending proposals to the government.

The one-month-old, six-party coalition government of Chavalit Yongchaiyudh on Tuesday approved a Finance Ministry proposal to slash the 1996/97 and 1997/98 (October-September) fiscal year budgets by 50 billion baht ($2.0 billion) each year in a bid to help the sagging economy.
Chavalit, who is also defence minister, said certain military expenditures would be put on hold and he would not consider new arms acquisition during the 1996/97 and 1997/98 fiscal year budgets.

Included among the projects likely to be shelved are a navy plan to buy 17 billion baht worth of submarines, an army proposal to spend 5.0 billion baht for a fleet of armoured personnel carriers and an airforce plan to buy a second squardron of F-18/A jet fighters equipped with Advanced Meduim Range Air to Air Missiles (AMRAAM).

"The army will strictly comply with government policy and for the sake well-being of the people nobody will press for what he wants," General Chetha Tanajaro, the army commander in chief told reporters.

"The army is well aware of the problem of the trade deficit and the current account deficit but we still have to propose our real needs to the government. It is up to the higher authorities to consider them," he added.
Thailand's current account deficit, one of the highest in the region, rose to a six-year high of 8.2 percent of gross domestic product in 1996 compared with 8.1 percent in 1995.

The army had planned to request an 80 billion baht ($3.2 billion) budget allocation for fiscal 1997/98, a senior army source told Reuters. The army received over 50 billion baht in funding for the current fiscal year.
He said the overall armed forces budget proposal is for about 1.6 trillion baht.
Proposals for fiscal 1997/98 must be presented to the Budget Bureau later this month.

The army also wants to buy 50,000 rifles to replace the ageing U.S.-made M-16A's and a fleet of tanks to replace British-made, Scorpion light tanks which have been in use for more than 20 years, he said.
